clue.text: Sounds like what you might need

definitions.text: Sounds like what you might need

parts.words: Sounds like what you might need
parts.note: said aloud, the phrase meaning under discussion is heard as a handkerchief-like paper you reach for when you sneeze

explanation.surface: A vague remark about something you might require, with a hint that it is all in how it is said.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer means 'being debated', but spoken it is identical to 'a tissue', the thing you might need for a runny nose.
explanation.definitionFit: Pure pun: the phrase meaning under debate is pronounced exactly like a paper handkerchief.

clue.text: A northerner, of course

parts.note: a Scot comes from the north of Britain

explanation.surface: Someone from the north, naturally, as one might casually say.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of course' reads as 'naturally'; here 'course' alone is the definition, a racecourse. ASCOT is a famous English racecourse in Berkshire.
explanation.definitionFit: Ascot is a well-known racecourse, so it is an example of a course.

clue.text: Being stupid in a tiny way

indicators.note: taken as 'in a different way', it tells us to rearrange the preceding letters

explanation.surface: Behaving foolishly, but only slightly so.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in a tiny way' looks like it qualifies 'stupid'; the letters of IN A TINY are rearranged, signalled by 'way'.
explanation.definitionFit: Inanity is the quality or state of silliness and lack of sense, matching the noun phrase.

clue.text: OK to end on Mayday

indicators.note: in a down clue, 'on' places one piece after the other

parts.note: Mayday is the radio distress call, equivalent to SOS

indicators.note: the end of the word 'to' is its final letter

explanation.surface: Is it all right to finish on the first of May?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mayday' looks like the May holiday but is the distress call.
explanation.definitionFit: Something middling or passable is described as merely acceptable, the sense of OK.

clue.text: Revolutionary Karl Marx 50% income tax!

indicators.note: revolutionary suggests overturning, so the letters that follow are thrown into a new order
50% of the four-letter surname keeps only its first half

explanation.surface: An outraged cry that Marx would impose a 50 percent tax on income.
explanation.walkthrough: The fodder is KARL, MA (half of MARX), INCOME and TAX. The definition is the punctuation mark that ends the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: The printed symbol at the end of the clue is the punctuation for an exclamation, so it defines its own name.

clue.text: Fingers in many pies trapped

indicators.note: the word pies holds the other pieces trapped inside it

parts.note: K stands for a thousand, a large number

explanation.surface: Someone meddling, fingers in many pies, gets caught.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fingers in many pies' recalls the idiom for meddling; 'in' and 'many' (K, a thousand) go inside PIES.
explanation.definitionFit: Pinkies are little fingers, an informal plural for the smallest digits.

clue.text: Beautiful people lead ridiculous hunt sabotage

indicators.note: the lead of a word is its first letter
to sabotage is to wreck, so the letters are broken up and rebuilt

explanation.surface: Attractive protesters lead an absurd effort to disrupt a hunt.
explanation.walkthrough: P, the leading letter of 'people', is followed by a rearrangement of RIDICULOUS HUNT.
explanation.definitionFit: Pulchritudinous is a formal, rather comic word for physically attractive or lovely.

clue.text: Weak passage in Vietnam by Pam Bygraves

indicators.note: passage in says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A feeble stretch in a book about Vietnam written by one Pam Bygraves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'passage' looks like a section of writing; it signals a run of letters inside the following words.
explanation.definitionFit: Namby-pamby describes something feeble, sentimental or lacking vigour, a synonym of feeble.

clue.text: Available for purchase, now or in the future

definitions.meaning: goods inside a shop can be bought there
something awaiting you, coming later, as in a surprise to come

explanation.surface: Goods you can buy now, or will be able to later.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means both stocked inside a shop and lying ahead, as in a surprise to come.

clue.text: Confidence in battle of the Home Counties?

parts.note: the Home Counties surround London in the South East, SE
Crécy was a 1346 battle of the Hundred Years' War

explanation.surface: Trust placed in some clash fought around London.
explanation.walkthrough: The Home Counties are the counties around London, in England's South East; CRECY is the 1346 English victory in France.
explanation.definitionFit: Keeping something in confidence means keeping it private, which is the state of secretiveness.

clue.text: Generalissimo welcomed female compiler, relaxed with the Guardian and listened to this?

indicators.note: the commander's letters take in, or welcome, everything else

parts.note: a generalissimo is the commander-in-chief, abbreviated CIC
a lass is a girl
the setter refers to themself as I
calm means relaxed
the newspaper speaking of itself says us

explanation.surface: A dictator entertains a woman setter, at ease with the newspaper, while some music plays.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Generalissimo' is the commander-in-chief's abbreviation; the Guardian speaks of itself in the first person plural. 'welcomed' splits it around the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: The question mark signals a guess at what the relaxed company might be playing: orchestral works of the Western tradition.

clue.text: See 9
Success in borrowing rejected by Swiss capital option for sleeping partners

indicators.note: the victory word sits inside the turned-round loan word
rejected suggests being turned back, so the word is read in reverse

parts.note: borrowing leaves you in debt
a win is a success

indicators.note: the capital of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A financial tale of loans refused by a Swiss bank, with a hint of bedroom arrangements.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swiss capital' looks like Bern or Swiss money; it is just the S. 'rejected' turns DEBT into TBED, which WIN enters.
explanation.definitionFit: A pair of single beds is a choice for a couple who would rather sleep apart.

clue.text: Like the blubber in Homer's lacy pants

indicators.note: pants as British slang for rubbish, or as a verb of disorder, tells us to scramble the letters

parts.note: taken with its S, as written

explanation.surface: Describing the fat in Homer Simpson's lacy underwear, a comic image.
explanation.walkthrough: 'blubber' looks like fat but means someone crying; 'pants' signals rearranging HOMERS LACY.
explanation.definitionFit: Lachrymose means tearful or given to weeping, like a person who blubbers.

clue.text: International waters in effect from 12 August

parts.note: an open competition is open to all nations' entrants
seas are bodies of water
something switched on is in effect

explanation.surface: Maritime rules that apply from a particular date in August.
explanation.walkthrough: 12 August is the 'Glorious Twelfth', when grouse shooting begins in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: The period when hunting a game bird becomes legal starts on the Glorious Twelfth for British grouse.

clue.text: Contacts needed for this compiler's taking drugs without setback

parts.note: the setter's own, belonging to me

indicators.note: without means the following letters are taken away

parts.note: opiates are narcotic drugs
read as 'set' backwards

explanation.surface: A setter takes narcotics without suffering a relapse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'setback' is read as two words, 'set' turned back; 'Contacts' look like acquaintances but are contact lenses.
explanation.definitionFit: Short-sightedness is the eye condition corrected by contact lenses.

clue.text: Visualisation of shimmering mirage at the end of the valley

indicators.note: shimmering suggests a wavering, shifting image, so the letters move about
the final letter of the word valley

explanation.surface: A desert vision: a shimmering mirage at the far end of the valley.
explanation.definitionFit: Imagery is mental pictures, the act or product of picturing things in the mind.

clue.text: Smuggle in blossom, one in Africa

indicators.note: the smuggling word goes into the flower word

parts.note: a bud is a flower about to blossom
to run goods is to smuggle them
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Contraband hidden in flowers, one shipment somewhere in Africa.
explanation.definitionFit: Burundi is a small East African country, so it is a place found on that continent.

clue.text: They divert the movement of foxes

definitions.meaning: plates or screens that deflect the flow of air, sound or liquid
to fox someone is to puzzle or confuse them

explanation.surface: Hunt saboteurs' devices that send foxes in another direction.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun is a deflecting screen; the verb means to perplex, as foxes does.

clue.text: A bit of 9 10's demeanour went off without me

indicators.note: went off suggests something exploded or spoiled, so the letters are rearranged
the letters of me are excluded from the anagram pool

explanation.surface: Someone's demeanour soured when the speaker was absent.
explanation.walkthrough: DEMEANOUR minus M and E leaves DEANOUR, which 'went off' rearranges; 9 10 is CLASSICAL MUSIC.
explanation.definitionFit: A rondeau is a musical form with a recurring refrain, a piece from the orchestral repertoire.

clue.text: At first, Eva Braun could be sophisticated

indicators.note: could be suggests what the letters might become when rearranged
at first means taking the first letter of Eva

explanation.surface: Hitler's companion Eva Braun was once refined, it suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: Urbane describes someone suave, courteous and polished in manner.

clue.text: Requiring manipulation of the audience

indicators.note: what the audience hears, so the word is taken by its sound

parts.note: kneading is working dough or muscle with the hands

explanation.surface: A demand for crowd manipulation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'manipulation' looks like controlling people; it is the kneading of dough, which listeners hear as the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Needing and requiring both mean having a necessity for something.

clue.text: It's partly digital if learning, or life, rang in exchange

indicators.note: in exchange means the letters swap places among themselves

explanation.surface: A rambling conditional about learning, life and a phone ringing in an exchange.
explanation.walkthrough: Two fodders work: IF LEARNING, or (as the clue says) LIFE RANG IN, each rearranged by 'exchange'. 'digital' means of a finger.
explanation.definitionFit: The horny plate at a finger's tip is a part of a digit, hence partly digital.

clue.text: See 11
Pansy among daffodils is symbolic

indicators.note: among says the letters sit inside the run of words that follow

explanation.surface: A flower placed among daffodils carries symbolic meaning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pansy' looks like the flower beside the daffodils; it is a dated, derogatory word for a weak man.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are old-fashioned insults for a man thought weak or effeminate, so they are synonyms.

clue.text: Honesty can be disregarded; that's grim

indicators.note: words that are disregarded are left out

parts.note: candour is frankness

explanation.surface: Ignoring the truth makes for a bleak outlook.
explanation.definitionFit: Dour means stern and gloomy in manner, the same as forbidding.

clue.text: City is at the cutting edge in broadcasting

indicators.note: broadcasting is transmission by sound, so the word heard counts

parts.note: something at the forefront leads the field

explanation.surface: A city boasting that it pioneers in broadcasting.
explanation.walkthrough: LEEDS is a city in Yorkshire, northern England.
explanation.definitionFit: Leeds is a large city in West Yorkshire, an example of a city.

clue.text: A game English soldier's bagged — sorry

parts.note: polo is a game played on horseback

indicators.note: bagged means the soldier's letters hold the English letter

parts.note: a GI is an American soldier; GI'S gives the S

explanation.surface: An English soldier has captured a game and offers regrets.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying sorry is an apology, and the plural is the conventional expression of regret.

clue.text: Backwards family with sheep triggered the space race

indicators.note: backwards tells us to read the combined pieces from right to left

parts.note: kin are one's family
tups are rams, male sheep

explanation.surface: A rural family with their flock somehow sparked the space race.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1957 Soviet satellite launch alarmed the West and began the competition to reach space.

clue.text: Start to scream and shout about a horse being emaciated

indicators.note: the start of scream is its first letter
the cry goes about, around, the other letters

parts.note: to cry is to shout
GG, gee-gee, is a child's word for a horse

explanation.surface: Someone screams and yells at a horse that is starving.
explanation.definitionFit: Scraggy means thin and bony, as is something wasted from hunger.
